passages.title: Bees in the City
passages.text:
**A** Beekeeping is no longer only a country hobby. In cities such as London, Paris and New York, people keep beehives on rooftops, balconies and even in small back gardens. Some city halls and hotels have their own hives, and the honey is sold in their shops or served at breakfast.

**B** City bees may seem out of place, but in some ways cities suit them well. Parks, gardens and tree-lined streets offer a wide variety of flowers that bloom at different times of year. In the countryside, by contrast, large fields often contain just one crop, which flowers for only a few weeks.

**C** Cities are also warmer than the surrounding countryside, especially at night, because buildings and roads store heat. This means that the season when flowers are open can begin earlier in spring and last longer into autumn. Bees can therefore collect food for more weeks each year.

**D** However, experts warn that too many hives in one area can cause problems. Honeybees compete with wild bees, such as bumblebees, for the same flowers. If there are not enough flowers for all of them, wild bees may suffer, and some of these species are already rare.

**E** For this reason, some cities now encourage residents to plant more flowers rather than add more hives. A single window box of lavender or a corner of a garden left to grow wild can provide food for many kinds of insects. As one beekeeper put it, 'Bees need flowers first, and honey comes later.'

passages.title: The Sea Otter
passages.text:
**A** Sea otters live along the coasts of the northern Pacific Ocean, from Japan to California. Unlike most sea mammals, they have no thick layer of fat to keep them warm. Instead, they rely on their fur, which is the densest of any animal, with up to one million hairs in a single square inch.

**B** Because cold water quickly takes heat from the body, sea otters must eat a great deal. An adult may eat food equal to about a quarter of its body weight every day. Its diet includes sea urchins, crabs, clams and other animals that live on the sea floor.

**C** Sea otters are one of the few animals known to use tools. Floating on its back, an otter places a flat stone on its chest and strikes a shellfish against it until the shell breaks. Some otters keep a favourite stone in a loose pocket of skin under the arm.

**D** In the 1700s and 1800s, sea otters were hunted for their valuable fur, and by the early 1900s only a few thousand remained. An international agreement in 1911 protected them, and their numbers slowly began to recover in many areas.

**E** Scientists now know that sea otters play an important role in their environment. By eating sea urchins, which feed on kelp, otters help underwater kelp forests to grow. These forests provide shelter for many species of fish.

passages.title: Why Schools Should Teach Cooking
passages.text:
**A** In many countries, cooking has quietly disappeared from the school timetable. I believe this is a mistake. Knowing how to prepare a simple, healthy meal is as useful as any skill a young person can learn, and schools are the best place to teach it.

**B** Some people argue that cooking should be taught at home. In an ideal world, perhaps it would be. But many parents work long hours and rely on ready meals, and children who never see food being prepared cannot be expected to learn by themselves.

**C** Cooking lessons also support other subjects. Measuring ingredients involves maths, and understanding why bread rises is a lesson in science. In my experience, students who struggle in a normal classroom often concentrate better when they can work with their hands.

**D** Critics point to the cost of kitchens and ingredients. These costs are real, but they are small compared with the long-term costs of poor diets, which are linked to illnesses that are expensive to treat. A basic kitchen classroom is a sensible investment.

**E** I am not suggesting that every student should become a chef. The aim is more modest: to make sure that no one leaves school unable to boil an egg or cook a pan of vegetables. That, surely, is not too much to ask.

passages.title: Drinking Water from the Sea
passages.text:
**A** About 97 percent of the water on Earth is salty, and most of the remaining fresh water is locked in ice or underground. As populations grow and droughts become more frequent, many countries are turning to the sea itself as a source of drinking water through a process called desalination.

**B** The oldest method of removing salt from water is distillation: seawater is heated until it turns to steam, and the steam is cooled and collected as fresh water, leaving the salt behind. Sailors used simple versions of this technique for centuries. However, boiling large amounts of water requires enormous quantities of energy.

**C** Most modern plants instead use a method called reverse osmosis. Seawater is pushed at high pressure through membranes with pores so small that water molecules can pass through but salt cannot. Improvements in membranes and pumps have greatly reduced the energy needed, although desalinated water is still usually more expensive than water from rivers or underground sources.

**D** Desalination also raises environmental concerns. For every litre of fresh water produced, plants discharge roughly one and a half litres of brine, a liquid far saltier than seawater. If this brine is released carelessly, it can sink to the sea floor and harm the organisms that live there. Some plants now dilute the brine or spread it through many small outlets.

**E** Despite these challenges, desalination is expanding rapidly, particularly in the Middle East, where some countries obtain most of their drinking water from the sea. Researchers are also experimenting with plants powered by solar energy, which could make the process cleaner and cheaper in sunny, dry regions.

passages.title: Lichens: Partners in Survival
passages.text:
**A** Lichens are among the most widespread living things on Earth, yet few people notice them. They grow as crusty patches on rocks, leafy growths on tree bark and tufts hanging from branches, and they can be found everywhere from tropical forests to the frozen deserts of Antarctica.

**B** For a long time, scientists believed that a lichen was a single organism. In the nineteenth century, however, the Swiss botanist Simon Schwendener proposed that each lichen is in fact a partnership between a fungus and an alga or a type of bacterium that can photosynthesise. His idea was strongly opposed at first, but it is now accepted.

**C** In this partnership, the fungus provides a protective structure and absorbs water and minerals, while its partner uses sunlight to produce sugars that feed both. This cooperation allows lichens to survive in places where neither partner could live alone, such as bare rock or extremely cold mountain tops.

**D** Lichens grow very slowly, sometimes only a millimetre a year. Because some species grow at a known, steady rate, geologists have used them to estimate how long ago rock surfaces were exposed, for example after a glacier retreated. This method, called lichenometry, works best for surfaces that are a few hundred years old.

**E** Lichens are also sensitive to air pollution, especially sulphur dioxide. In the industrial cities of the nineteenth century, many species disappeared. Today, scientists survey lichens to monitor air quality, and the return of sensitive species to some cities has been taken as a sign that the air has become cleaner.

passages.title: The Case for Learning Latin
passages.text:
**A** When I tell people that I teach Latin, they often ask why anyone should learn a language that nobody speaks. It is a fair question. My answer is that Latin is useful not because students will speak it, but because of what learning it does to the way they think about language.

**B** Latin is a highly inflected language: the endings of words change to show their role in a sentence. To read even a simple sentence, students must analyse each word carefully. I have found that this habit of close attention carries over to their reading and writing in English.

**C** Supporters of Latin often claim that it improves students' vocabulary, since many English words come from Latin roots. This is true, but I think the claim is overstated. Students can learn these roots in a few lessons; they do not need years of study to discover that 'aqua' means water.

**D** A stronger argument is that Latin opens a door to a long literary tradition. Reading Virgil or Ovid in the original is a different experience from reading a translation, and students who manage it gain a confidence that few other achievements provide.

**E** None of this means that Latin should be compulsory. Many students will gain more from studying a modern language that allows them to talk to people in other countries. But for those who enjoy puzzles and patterns, Latin deserves a place in the curriculum.

passages.title: Radiocarbon Dating and Its Limits
passages.text:
**A** Living things constantly take in carbon from the atmosphere, including a small proportion of carbon-14, a radioactive form of the element. When an organism dies, it stops absorbing carbon, and the carbon-14 it contains begins to decay at a steady rate, halving roughly every 5,730 years. By measuring how much carbon-14 remains in a sample of bone, wood or cloth, scientists can estimate how long ago the organism died.

**B** The technique, developed by the American chemist Willard Libby in the late 1940s, transformed archaeology. For the first time, researchers could assign dates to objects from prehistoric sites that had left no written records. Libby received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1960 for the work.

**C** Early users of the method assumed that the amount of carbon-14 in the atmosphere had always been constant. It soon became clear that this was not the case: levels have varied over time because of changes in the sun's activity and in Earth's magnetic field. Raw radiocarbon ages must therefore be 'calibrated' against records from objects of known age, such as tree rings, which can be counted year by year.

**D** Human activity has complicated matters further. Since the Industrial Revolution, the burning of fossil fuels, which contain no carbon-14, has diluted the proportion of carbon-14 in the air, while nuclear weapons tests in the 1950s and 1960s temporarily almost doubled it. Samples from these periods therefore require special treatment.

**E** The method also has a natural limit. After about 50,000 years, so little carbon-14 remains that it can no longer be measured reliably. For older materials, scientists must turn to other techniques, such as those based on the decay of potassium or uranium, which can date rocks millions or even billions of years old.

passages.title: How Animals Sleep
passages.text:
**A** Almost every animal that has been carefully studied shows some form of sleep, a state of reduced activity and responsiveness from which it can be woken. Yet the amount and pattern of sleep vary enormously. Some bats sleep for around twenty hours a day, while adult elephants in the wild have been recorded sleeping for only about two hours.

**B** Many marine mammals face a particular challenge: they must surface to breathe. Dolphins solve this problem by resting one half of the brain at a time. During this 'unihemispheric' sleep, one eye remains open and the animal continues to swim slowly, apparently keeping watch for predators and staying close to its group.

**C** Some birds do something similar. Studies of frigatebirds, which can stay at sea for weeks without landing, found that they sleep while flying, often with one half of the brain at a time and for only a few seconds at once. In total, they slept less than an hour a day in flight, far less than they did on land.

**D** Why sleep exists at all remains a puzzle. A sleeping animal cannot feed, mate or easily escape danger, so sleep must provide important benefits to have survived in so many species. Leading theories suggest that sleep helps to save energy, to repair tissues, and to strengthen memories by reorganising connections in the brain.

**E** Evidence that sleep is essential comes from experiments in which animals are deprived of it. Even fruit flies that are kept awake show reduced learning, and when finally allowed to rest, they sleep longer and more deeply than usual, as if paying back a debt. Such findings suggest that sleep serves functions that cannot simply be postponed.

passages.title: The Myth of Multitasking
passages.text:
**A** We like to believe that we can do several things at once: answer emails during a meeting, listen to a podcast while studying, check messages while driving. I want to argue that, for most tasks that require thought, multitasking is largely an illusion, and an expensive one.

**B** What feels like doing two things simultaneously is usually rapid switching between them. Each switch carries a small cost, as the brain disengages from one set of rules and loads another. Individually these costs are tiny, but they accumulate, and studies consistently find that people who switch frequently take longer and make more errors than those who complete tasks one at a time.

**C** Defenders of multitasking point out that some combinations work well. Walking while talking, or listening to music while washing dishes, seems to cause few problems. This is true, but it does not contradict my argument. These examples pair an automatic activity with one that requires attention; the difficulty arises when both tasks demand conscious thought.

**D** Perhaps the most troubling finding is that people who multitask heavily are often the most confident in their ability to do so, even though their performance is no better, and sometimes worse, than that of others. Our sense of being productive, in other words, is a poor guide to whether we actually are.

**E** I am not suggesting that we can always avoid interruptions; modern work rarely allows that. But we can choose to protect periods of uninterrupted concentration for our most demanding tasks. The evidence suggests that doing so is not a luxury but one of the simplest ways to work better.
